Garlic-Sesame Galbisal

Galbisal is the boneless strip off the rib — all of the galbi flavor, none of the bone, and it grills faster than its flanken cousin (#M03).

Korean · Easy · Serves 4

Jump to recipe ↓
Chapter 01 / 20 meat recipes ↗

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: restaurant. Galbisal is the boneless strip off the rib — all of the galbi flavor, none of the bone, and it grills faster than its flanken cousin (#M03). The classic restaurant treatment keeps the marinade short and quiet: garlic, sesame oil, soy, a thread of sweetness, black pepper. The meat is the argument; the marinade is the microphone. This is the record for the table that wants galbi flavor on a weeknight clock, and for the grill boss who is tired of managing sugar on the fire — there is barely any here to burn.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Keep the marinade thick and the marinate short. Grated garlic carries the flavor load; whisk everything into a loose paste, coat the slices by hand, and refrigerate 2–4 hours. Past that the sesame oil starts carrying off the beef's own scent — this lane's ceiling is shorter than the sweet marinades.
  • While the grill heats: toast an extra pinch of sesame seeds in a dry pan for the finish. Thirty seconds of work the whole table will taste.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Charcoal or cast-iron at medium-high. The slices go on in a single layer, and because there is almost no sugar, the grill boss's job is color, not lacquer-management: leave them until the edges weep and the underside is browned, about 2 minutes. Checkpoint — the smell should be sesame and garlic over browning beef — a quieter grill smell than the sweet marinades, and the honest one for this cut.
  2. 02
    Flip once, 90 seconds more, pull when the raw red is just gone at the center of the slice. Rest the batch 1 minute on a warm plate — galbisal is thin enough that carryover is quick and real. Checkpoint — eating test straight off the grill: beef first, garlic second, sesame after. If you taste marinade before meat, the soy ran heavy — pull back a teaspoon next batch.
  3. 03
    Scissors into bite pieces, warm platter, sesame over, ssam station open. The purist dip here is gireumjang (#SA02) — sesame oil, salt, pepper — because it seasons without competing; ssamjang (#SA01) for the bolder table. Checkpoint — the ssam test: leaf, gireumjang, galbisal, fold — and it should taste like the steakhouse version of Korean grill, clean enough that the beef's quality is the headline. Buy the good beef for this one; there is nowhere to hide. Chef’s Note — galbisal is the cut that exposes your butcher. With no overnight slurry and no sugar lacquer, everything the slice tastes like is the meat plus garlic and sesame — so this is the record where spending up on well-marbled beef visibly pays, and where the frozen-cheap stuff visibly fails. Same reason the restaurant tables put it on the menu beside the bone-in: it is the connoisseur's order, not the beginner's.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Bland despite marinadeSoy too light or beef wateryFull-salt soy; pat slices dry before marinating
Garlic burned bitterGrated garlic on a too-hot grateMedium-high, not rocket; 2-minute first side
Slices toughCut with the grainRe-slice against the grain; 5 mm max
Marinade pooled wateryOver-marinated or wet beef2–4 hours only; dry the slices first

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Marinated slices keep 24 hours refrigerated. Cooked, 3 days — cold slices over rice with a fried egg and the leftover gireumjang is the intended day-after move.
  • Variations: a teaspoon of gochugaru in the marinade for a slow heat; the mushroom-soy build (#M02) swaps in cleanly; the bone-in flanken fork (#M03) when the table wants the full ceremony.
